objects: binary phenotype; observed and liability scales
conclusion: Disease status is measured on the 0-1 scale whereas heritability is most interpretable on a liability scale.
span: Scale. For quantitative traits the scale of measurement is the same as the scale on which heritability is expressed. For disease traits, the phenotypes (case-control status) are measured on the 0–1 scale, but heritability is most interpretable on a scale of liability.

objects: y; mu; u; e; V=A sigma_u^2 + I sigma_e^2
assumptions: binary observations; SNP-derived realized relationship matrix A
conclusion: The observed binary phenotype is modeled with additive SNP effects and residuals having covariance V=A sigma_u^2+I sigma_e^2.
span: The variance structure of phenotypic observations is written as $\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{A}{\sigma }_{u}^{2}+\mathbf{I}{\sigma }_{e}^{2}$, where A is the realized relationship matrix estimated from SNP data, I is an identity matrix, ${\sigma }_{u}^{2}$ is polygenic additive genetic variance explained by the SNPs, and ${\sigma }_{e}^{2}$ is error variance; these variances are on the observed 0–1 scale.
location: lee_2011 | PMC journal version (2011) | Material and Methods > Linear Mixed Model

objects: individual SNP genotypes; allele frequencies; realized relationships
assumptions: dense genome-wide SNP data from conventionally unrelated individuals
conclusion: Realized additive relationships are estimated from heterozygosity-scaled products of individual genotype indicators across SNPs.
scope: Individual-level genotype input, not GWAS summary statistics.
span: We showed previously that it is possible to estimate realized relationships between unrelated (in a conventional sense) individuals from dense SNP data.^{7} A simple and logical method of estimating realized additive genetic relationships (${\widehat{A}}_{ij}$) between individual i and j is to use the products of genotype indicator coefficients between two individuals scaled by the heterozygosity for all L genotyped SNPs across the genome,^{7}

assumptions: linear mixed model for observed disease status
conclusion: Observed-scale heritability is the additive variance fraction, with variance components estimated by REML.
scope: Variance-component estimation rather than individual SNP significance testing.
span: Therefore, the heritability on the observed scale is ${h}_{o}^{2}={\sigma }_{u}^{2}/\left({\sigma }_{u}^{2}+{\sigma }_{e}^{2}\right)$, the ratio of total phenotypic variance on that scale that is due to additive genetic effects. The variance components are estimated via residual maximum likelihood (REML) analysis.^{4,15,16}
location: lee_2011 | PMC journal version (2011) | Material and Methods > Linear Mixed Model

objects: liability l; genetic component g; residual e
assumptions: unascertained population; unit total liability variance
conclusion: Liability is standard normal and its additive genetic component is normal with variance sigma_g^2.
scope: Population liability model; ascertainment changes the sampled distribution.
span: where l is a vector of liability phenotypes that are distributed as N(0, 1), g is a vector of random additive genetic effects on the liability scale that are distributed N(0, ${\sigma }_{g}^{2}$), and other terms are the same as in the linear model but on the liability scale. We note that the mean of the distribution of liability is zero (μ = 0) when there is no ascertainment.
location: lee_2011 | PMC journal version (2011) | Material and Methods > Liability Threshold Model

conclusion: Liability is assumed to be the sum of independent normally distributed environmental and additive genetic components.
scope: Random-effect distribution assumption, not a fitted Bayesian shrinkage prior.
span: One can model the relationship between observations on the observed risk scale and liabilities on the unobserved continuous scale by using a probit transformation to generate the classical liability threshold model^{6} (Figure 1). Liability of disease is assumed to be the sum of environmental and additive genetic components from independent normal distributions.

objects: h_l^2; estimated h_o,cc^2; population prevalence K; sample case fraction P; threshold density z
assumptions: liability model; REML observed-scale estimate; ascertainment correction; specified K and P
conclusion: For reporting, observed-scale SNP heritability is converted to population liability-scale heritability by multiplying by K^2(1-K)^2/[z^2 P(1-P)].
scope: SNP-attributable population liability variance, not total pedigree heritability.
span: In the absence of ascertainment (P = K), this equation reduces to Equation 17, hence adjusting for ascertainment when variance components are estimated by maximum likelihood leads to a generalization of the classical Robertson transformation. Equation 23 shows the transformation that needs to be applied to the SNP-attributable variance estimated from Equation 9 to provide an estimate of the liability variance in the total population explained by the SNPs.

assumptions: P=K for the reduction; maximum-likelihood variance-component estimation
conclusion: The ascertainment-corrected transformation generalizes the classical Robertson transformation and reduces to it when P=K.
span: In the absence of ascertainment (P = K), this equation reduces to Equation 17, hence adjusting for ascertainment when variance components are estimated by maximum likelihood leads to a generalization of the classical Robertson transformation. Equation 23 shows the transformation that needs to be applied to the SNP-attributable variance estimated from Equation 9 to provide an estimate of the liability variance in the total population explained by the SNPs.

objects: additive and nonadditive genetic variance; Robertson transformation
assumptions: family estimates include nonadditive variation; distant relatives have comparatively little nonadditive covariance
conclusion: The Robertson transformation can bias family-data estimates, while distant-relative estimates give a good approximation when nonadditive variation is relatively small.
scope: Approximation for distant relatives; ascertainment requires further correction.
span: This linear transformation was derived by Alan Robertson in the Appendix of Dempster and Lerner.^{18} When applied to estimates of genetic variation on the observed scale derived from family data, this transformation can give biased estimates on the liability scale because the genetic variation estimable from close relatives contains both additive and nonadditive variance.^{18,19} However, when the genetic variance is estimated from distant relatives, the nonadditive genetic component of the variance is small relative to the additive component, and so the Robertson transformation provides a good approximation.
location: lee_2011 | PMC journal version (2011) | Material and Methods > Liability Threshold Model

objects: liability-scale heritability estimate; disease prevalence K
assumptions: paper simulation design: 5000 cases and 5000 controls; independent batches with low relatedness; normal liability components
conclusion: Ascertainment-corrected estimates were largely unbiased in the simulations, with slight overestimation at K=0.001.
scope: Simulation-supported calibration, not an unrestricted finite-sample theorem.
span: When ascertained case-control studies were used, the estimates were largely unbiased although a slight overestimation was observed for an extreme value of K = 0.001 (Table 1).
location: lee_2011 | PMC journal version (2011) | Results > Simulations

objects: population prevalence K; liability-scale SNP variance
conclusion: The liability-scale variance estimate relies on knowledge of population disease prevalence.
scope: Prevalence uncertainty is an input limitation rather than a tunable shrinkage setting.
span: Our estimate of the proportion of variation in liability that is tagged by all SNPs relies on knowledge of the population prevalence (K), just as it does when one estimates total heritability of liability from pedigree or twin analyses by using binary traits.

objects: tagged variance; common and rare causal variants
assumptions: variance detected through LD with genotyped SNPs
conclusion: The method cannot distinguish whether detected variance tags common or rare causal variants.
scope: Identifiability limitation of the aggregate variance estimate.
span: Our method cannot differentiate between whether the variance detected represents LD with causal variants that are common or rare.

objects: GLMM; maximum likelihood; integration approximations; ascertainment
assumptions: binary-trait GLMMs using the cited numerical-integration approximations
conclusion: The authors contrast their LMM approach with approximate maximum-likelihood GLMMs, reporting serious approximation bias and lack of case-control ascertainment correction in those GLMM methods.
scope: Author-stated comparison of the cited GLMM methods.
span: However, generalized LMMs (GLMMs) that use maximum likelihood for estimation and approximations to avoid numerical integration^{30} and that have been widely used for binary traits have a problem of serious bias induced by the approximations.^{31} In addition, these methods do not take account of ascertainment typical of case-control studies.

objects: genotype indicators x; allele frequency p; reference population
assumptions: current population is the reference population for relatedness
conclusion: As in Yang et al., relatedness is defined using the current population as the base population with expected genotype count 2p.
span: where x_{il} = 0, 1, or 2 according to whether individual i has genotype bb, Bb, or BB at locus l (alleles are arbitrarily called b or B), p (q) is allele frequency of B (b), and 2p is the mean of x_{l}. As in Yang et al.,^{7} we use the current population as the base (reference) population when estimating relatedness from SNP data so that E(x) = 2p in the current population.

objects: REML variance estimate; predicted genetic values; normality
assumptions: REML derivation of the scale transformation
conclusion: The REML variance derivation invokes a normality assumption and a phenotype-on-predictor regression slope of one.
scope: Stated derivation premise; ascertained liability is not itself normally distributed.
span: The REML estimate of the genetic variance (${\widehat{\sigma }}_{u}^{2}$ or ${\widehat{\sigma }}_{{u}_{cc}}^{2}$) is the covariance between observations and the unbiased estimate of the genetic values ($\widehat{u}$ or ${\widehat{u}}_{cc}$) with a normality assumption, that is, the regression of phenotype on predictor has a slope of 1, $\mathrm{cov}\left(y,\widehat{u}\right)/{\widehat{\sigma }}_{u}^{2}=1$ or $\mathrm{cov}\left({y}_{cc},{\widehat{u}}_{cc}\right)/{\widehat{\sigma }}_{{u}_{cc}}^{2}=1$.
location: lee_2011 | PMC journal version (2011) | Material and Methods > Ascertainment-Corrected Transformation
